A constant horizontal force acts on a block moving along a frictionless surface. Its kinetic energy increases by ΔK₁ while moving from x = 0 to 50 cm, and by ΔK₂ while moving from 50 cm to 100 cm. Which statement is correct?

A. ΔK₂ = ΔK₁ because the speed increases by the same amount in each interval.
B. ΔK₂ = ΔK₁ because the force does equal work over the two intervals.
C. ΔK₂ > ΔK₁ because the block moves faster in the second interval.
D. ΔK₂ > ΔK₁ because the rate of energy transfer is larger in the second interval.

answer.text: B. The work is FΔx, which is equal for equal displacements under the same force. By the work–energy theorem the kinetic-energy increases are equal.

Compare the changes in mechanical energy of (i) the blocks–spring system and (ii) the blocks–spring–Earth system.

A. (i) increases; (ii) decreases
B. (i) decreases; (ii) increases
C. (i) is unchanged; (ii) decreases
D. Both are unchanged

answer.text: A. The first system gains spring potential energy and has zero kinetic energy at both endpoints. Including Earth also includes gravitational potential energy; some of that energy is dissipated by friction, so its total mechanical energy decreases.

answer.text: B. k_X = 20/0.10 = 200 N m⁻¹ and k_Y = 80/0.05 = 1600 N m⁻¹. At equal extension, E = ½kx² makes E_Y/E_X = 8. At equal force, E = F²/(2k), so Y would store only one eighth of X’s energy.

Which statement about efficiency is correct?

B. The joule is a unit of efficiency.

cross-ap24p1-written-1a-b:whole.hint: Account for the potential energy that remains at B.
notes: Only the loss in gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy. The track shape does not affect this calculation if friction is negligible.

cross-ap24p1-written-5a:whole.hint: The kinetic-energy gain is supplied; you do not need to reconstruct the collision.
notes: Since the block was initially at rest, its final kinetic energy equals the stated gain. Momentum data for the other block are unnecessary.

cross-ap1ced-mcq-3:whole.hint: Compare the distance over which the force acts, rather than the time taken.
notes: Work measures energy transferred; power measures its rate. Greater speed can increase power without increasing the work done over a fixed distance.

cross-ap1ced-mcq-10:whole.hint: List which potential energies belong inside each stated system.
notes: Gravitational potential energy belongs to the blocks–Earth interaction. Mechanical energy excludes the thermal energy produced by friction, although total energy is conserved.

cross-ca25n12-mcq-17:whole.hint: The factor one half in kinetic energy does not mean the work done by every force is one half force times distance.
notes: A constant-force graph has a rectangular area Fs. A triangular area ½Fx applies to a force increasing linearly from zero, as for stretching an initially relaxed spring.

cross-ca25n12-mcq-18:whole.hint: Potential energy depends on the initial and final heights, not the path between them.
notes: For a uniform gravitational field, ΔE_p = mg(h_final − h_initial). The total vertical distance travelled is not the height change.

cross-ca25n12-mcq-19:whole.hint: Make an energy balance with input work, thermal energy and gravitational potential energy.
notes: Use distance along the slope for work by the parallel pushing force and vertical height for gravitational potential energy. Weight is already given in newtons: do not multiply it by g again.

cross-ca25n12-mcq-20:whole.hint: Convert the rate of height gain to metres per second before using energy transferred per second.
notes: Constant speed means kinetic energy is unchanged. Useful lifting power is the rate of gravitational potential-energy increase, not the electrical input unless efficiency is 100%.

cross-ca25n12-mcq-23:whole.hint: The force was not at its final value throughout the stretching. Use the area under a force–extension graph.
notes: The average force for a spring starting relaxed is half the final force. Convert both kN to N and cm to m before calculating energy.

cross-ca25j12-mcq-18:whole.hint: Use the work–energy theorem; the stopping distance is not needed to find the total energy change.
notes: The cushion’s work on the ball is negative because its force opposes the motion. Positive answer options describe the magnitude, not the signed work.

cross-ca25j12-mcq-19:whole.hint: Find the pushing distance along the slope, then subtract the gain in gravitational potential energy from the input work.
notes: Constant speed makes ΔE_k = 0. The pushing force acts along the slope, while the gravitational energy change uses vertical height. These are different distances.

cross-ca25j12-mcq-22:whole.hint: Find the ratio of spring constants, then choose an energy equation suited to what is held equal.
notes: A stiffer spring stores more energy at the same extension but less energy under the same applied force. Read the two graph scales separately; they are different.

cross-ca25m12-mcq-14:whole.hint: Identify the quantity in the work formula that can be replaced using velocity and time.
notes: P = Fv in this scalar form uses the force component along the motion. A perpendicular force does no work; more generally P = Fv cos θ.

cross-ca25m12-mcq-15:whole.hint: Find the vertical height change before equating the decrease in gravitational energy with the increase in kinetic energy.
notes: Slope length and vertical height are different. The mass cancels, and speed requires a square root because kinetic energy is proportional to v².

cross-ca25m12-mcq-16:whole.hint: Use the force and the displacement of its point of application in the force direction.
notes: The work of one force is not automatically the resultant work. No acceleration or mass calculation is needed when force and its displacement are already given.

cross-ca25m12-mcq-17:whole.hint: Convert the mass per minute to mass per second, then calculate the gravitational energy delivered each second.
notes: Efficiency multiplies the available input power. Watts are joules per second, so leaving the flow rate in kilograms per minute creates a factor-of-60 error.

cross-ca25m12-mcq-21:whole.hint: Read the compression at the force on one spring. The area under that spring’s force–compression graph gives its stored energy.
notes: Convert millimetres to metres when calculating energy in joules. Add the four spring energies after using the force on one spring, rather than using the total load twice.

cross-fast-ocr-1c4ec7fca86488ad-1-a4:who.hint: Use either force times braking distance or the loss of kinetic energy; keep the sign convention clear.
notes: The 37 m total stopping distance includes the reaction distance, during which the brakes do no work.
The work-energy theorem gives the same magnitude: ½mv² = 1.94×10⁵ J.

cross-fast-ocr-1c4ec7fca86488ad-3-c:whol.hint: Add the lost gravitational potential energy to the initial kinetic energy; no flight-time calculation is needed.
notes: With negligible air resistance, the ball’s mechanical energy is conserved between release and impact.
Kinetic energy depends on total speed, so using only the downward velocity would omit most of its energy.

cross-fast-ocr-1c4ec7fca86488ad-4-a4:who.hint: Replace the two series springs by their equivalent force constant before using elastic potential energy.
notes: The energy stored in both springs equals the energy of the equivalent spring for the same total extension.
Use metres for extension when the force constant is expressed in newtons per metre.

cross-fast-ocr-1c4ec7fca86488ad-4-b2:who.hint: Estimate the area below the curve to the 3.5 N endpoint, remembering that millimetres must become metres.
notes: Each graph area unit N·m is a joule, so the extension-axis conversion sets the power of ten.
The nonlinear area is best estimated with squares or several trapezia rather than one triangle.

cross-fast-vcaa-85b84de5ad48f3e7-7-whole.hint: Relate the work done by the constant braking force to the initial kinetic energy.
notes: Stopping distance is proportional to speed squared when mass and braking force are unchanged.
Using a simple speed ratio would miss the quadratic dependence of kinetic energy.

cross-fast-aqa-f44747ff7b639a5d-2-a3:who.hint: Use a = v(dv/dx) to turn the speed-distance slope into acceleration.
notes: Kinetic energy uses the speed squared: read the speed at 5600 m and convert the mass to kilograms before using ½mv².
Here dv/dx has units s⁻¹ and a = v(dv/dx). Useful accelerating power is mav; divide by the engine input power in the same units.

cross-fast-production-003-a-q17:whole.hint: Calculate work for the horizontal push and lift separately; use constant lifting velocity to find the vertical applied force.
notes: Constant velocity during the lift means zero resultant force, so the lifting force equals the 40 N weight.
The question asks for work by the two applied forces, giving 48 J + 64 J rather than net work on the box.

cross-fast-production-003-a-q18:whole.hint: Write efficiency as an output-to-input ratio and examine what happens to the units.
notes: Efficiency can be expressed as a decimal or percentage, but neither form is a physical unit.
Both energy-ratio and power-ratio definitions are dimensionless because numerator and denominator have matching units.

cross-fast-production-003-a-q20:whole.hint: Translate constant speed into kinetic energy, then relate a constant downward speed to height and gravitational potential energy.
notes: The ball loses gravitational potential energy even though its kinetic energy is constant; the lost energy is dissipated thermally in the oil.
A constant downward speed makes height decrease linearly with time, so mgh also decreases linearly.

cross-fast-production-003-a-q23:whole.hint: Use the area under a force-extension graph rather than trying to use the Young modulus distractor.
notes: The triangular area contains the factor one half because force increases from zero to its final value.
Young modulus alone cannot give the stored energy without the wire’s dimensions; E is not needed for this question.

cross-fast-production-004-a-q10:whole.hint: Apply conservation of mechanical energy from just after impact to the highest point.
notes: The supplied 10 m s⁻¹ is the checked post-collision speed, so do not repeat the momentum calculation.
At maximum height the speed is zero and the post-impact kinetic energy has become gravitational potential energy.

cross-fast-production-004-a-q14:whole.hint: Scale the resistive force with v², then use power equals force times steady speed.
notes: The force becomes four times larger when speed doubles because resistance is proportional to v².
At steady speed the driving force balances resistance, so the engine’s useful output power is Fv.

cross-fast-production-004-a-q15:whole.hint: Identify the useful vertical energy gain and divide it by the work done by the applied pull.
notes: Frictional work explains the lost energy but does not replace the total input Pd in the denominator.
Efficiency is useful output divided by total input, so the fraction must be less than or equal to one.

cross-fast-production-004-a-q16:whole.hint: Use the squared dependence of kinetic energy on speed and take the square root of the energy factor.
notes: Kinetic energy is not directly proportional to speed; it is proportional to speed squared.
The particle mass is unchanged, so it cancels when the two kinetic energies are compared.

cross-fast-production-004-a-q17:whole.hint: Convert grams to kilograms before applying ΔEₚ=mgh.
notes: Using 28 rather than 0.028 for mass makes the result one thousand times too large.
The energy change is positive because the mass is raised against gravity.

cross-fast-production-005-a-q16:whole.hint: Use the wasted 230 W as 26% of the input, then calculate the useful 74% share.
notes: The 230 W is the wasted portion, not the total input power, so it must be divided by 0.26.
Useful and wasted powers add to input power; rounding explains the listed 650 W option.

cross-fast-production-005-a-q17:whole.hint: Compare total kinetic-plus-gravitational energy at the two stated positions.
notes: The projectile gains gravitational potential energy while losing a larger amount of kinetic energy.
Work against air resistance equals the decrease in mechanical energy, so report a positive energy amount.

cross-fast-ocr-9b5d09d08cd2c050-6-whole:.hint: Resolve the tension along the direction of motion before multiplying force by speed.
notes: A perpendicular force component changes neither the displacement along the surface nor the motor’s rate of work on the load.
Constant speed means the horizontal forces balance, but the motor still transfers energy while overcoming resistance.

cross-fast-production-007-a-b07-a:whole.hint: Find the vertical drop before applying conservation of mechanical energy.
notes: The vertical drop from an angle θ to the bottom is L(1−cosθ).
String tension does no work because it is perpendicular to the instantaneous motion.

cross-fast-production-007-a-b09-a:whole.hint: Substitute mass and speed directly into translational kinetic energy.
notes: Square the speed before multiplying by half the mass.
This establishes energy available for the climb around the loop.
